confirmed.title: An Operator can rewrite step pricing by sending pricingConfigJson as an empty string, which gets past the E5 money guard
confirmed.scenario: EnsureMayWriteStepPricing treats a blank PricingConfigJson as 'not sent' (MoneyRedaction.cs:66 maps it to null), so an Operator's request passes the guard. The service then hands the original "" to the engine. WorkflowEngine.ApplyStepPricing (WorkflowEngine.cs:369-370) reads any non-null value as 'clear the stored config' and sets step.PricingConfigJson = null, then recomputes CalculatedCost. Steps to reproduce: a Merchant prices the current step as Combined with config {items:[{model:1,rate:100000},{model:0,rate:50000}]} on a 2x3 rug, so the cost is 650,000. An Operator (Floor) sends PUT /api/rugs/{rugId}/steps/{stepId}/pricing with body {"pricingConfigJson":""}. The result is 200, not 403. The stored combined config is wiped and the step cost drops to the single-model fallback (0 with no unit rate). Rug investment and provider balances change with it. POST .../advance and POST /api/rugs/bulk/advance accept the same body, and the bulk route clears the config on every selected rug. I confirmed this with a unit probe on an exported 2b5870c snapshot: RugManagementService.UpdateStepPricingAsync under a non-Business IMoneyVisibility returned normally, step.PricingConfigJson became null and CalculatedCost moved off 650,000.
confirmed.fix: Make the guard match what the engine does. In EnsureMayWriteStepPricing, count PricingConfigJson as a money member whenever it is non-null, including empty or whitespace, because the engine treats that as 'clear'. Alternatively, have the service turn a blank PricingConfigJson into null before ToAdvanceRequest when money.CanSeeMoney is false. Add a 403 test for {"pricingConfigJson":""} on the pricing, advance and bulk-advance routes.

I traced the code at 2b5870c and could not refute the finding. The guard and the engine read a blank PricingConfigJson in opposite ways, and nothing between the controller and the engine turns "" into null.

1. The guard lets it through. MoneyRedaction.cs:66 maps a blank or whitespace PricingConfigJson to null before EnsureMayWriteMoney. HasNoMoney (line 40) then counts it as "not sent", so a non-Business user is not stopped.
2. Floor can reach the routes. RugsApiController.cs:49, 53 and 75 (advance, pricing, bulk/advance) have no action-level policy. They inherit [Authorize(Policy = Policies.Floor)] from ApiControllerBase.cs:19, and Operator is in FloorRoles (Policies.cs). The global JSON setup has no converter that changes "" to null, and AdvanceRugStepRequest has no validator, so "" arrives in the service as "".
3. The service passes "" on unchanged. ApplyProviderRateAsync (RugManagementService.cs:612+) returns the request untouched when the provider is unchanged and the step already has explicit pricing (AppliedPricingModel is set, which is true for a Combined step). ToAdvanceRequest (line 669+) copies PricingConfigJson as is.
4. The engine wipes the config. WorkflowEngine.ApplyStepPricing has `if (request.PricingConfigJson is not null) step.PricingConfigJson = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(...) ? null : ...`, so "" clears the stored config. UpdateStepPricingAsync and AdvanceStepAsync then recompute CalculatedCost. CostCalculationService.ComputeBase only uses combined pricing when the JSON is non-blank. Otherwise ComputeSingle falls to `_ => rate` for Combined, i.e. AppliedUnitRate or DefaultUnitRate, so the cost moves away from the Merchant's combined total.
5. The pricing route works on any non-cancelled step, completed steps included. BulkAdvanceAsync checks request.Step once (line 449) and then applies the same "" to the current step of every selected rug.

Erratum E5 says to return 403 for any non-null money value from a non-Business user, and "" is non-null. The guard's own doc comment lists the combined config as a guarded money member. The real frontend always sends null (CostRuleEditor, RugWorkflowPanel, RugBulkToolbar, ListQuickAdvance), so exploiting this needs a hand-crafted request. An Operator can make one, since they hold a valid session and CSRF token. The result is that an Operator can destroy a Merchant's stored step pricing and change rug investment and provider balances, which the E5 guard is meant to prevent.

confirmed.title: The last-admin guard is check-then-write with no lock, so two admins demoting each other at the same time leave the tenant with no TenantAdmin
confirmed.scenario: A tenant has exactly two active TenantAdmins, A and B. At about the same moment, A submits /Users/Save to make B a Merchant and B submits /Users/Save to make A a Merchant. In A's request, EnsureAdminRemainsAsync counts the other active admins excluding B and finds {A}, so it passes. In B's request it counts the others excluding A and finds {B}, so it also passes. User has no concurrency token, the guard holds no lock and the database has no constraint, so both writes commit. Both stamps rotate and the tenant ends with zero TenantAdmins. Nobody can then reach /Users or /Settings, and the SystemAdmin UI has no user editing.
confirmed.fix: Run the last-admin check and the write under one serialization point. Options: a Postgres advisory lock or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the tenant's admin rows inside the same transaction, or a SERIALIZABLE transaction for role/IsActive changes. Re-check the count after the update and before commit, and throw DomainConflictException(LastAdmin) if it is zero.

votes.reason: The race is real. At 2b5870c the last-admin guard is a plain read followed by a later write. Nothing serializes the two, and nothing in the database backs it up. When two TenantAdmins demote or deactivate each other at nearly the same moment, both requests pass the check, both commit, and the tenant is left with no active TenantAdmin. The odds are low: it needs two different admins, each acting on the other, inside a window of a few to tens of milliseconds. A single admin can't cause it alone, because the self-demote guard at line 158 blocks it, and with three or more admins one always remains. Still, nothing in the code stops it, so the finding stands at low severity.

confirmed.title: Activity log paging overflows int for large ?page and returns 500 (negative OFFSET)
confirmed.scenario: ActivityLogService.ListAsync (line 37) only clamps the page from below (Math.Max(1, page)). PageAsync then computes `.Skip((page - 1) * pageSize)` in int. Repro: a TenantAdmin opens /Settings/Activity?page=80000000 (default PageSize 30). (80,000,000-1)*30 is above int.MaxValue, so the offset wraps negative and Postgres throws 2201X 'OFFSET must not be negative'. I reproduced this on a throwaway DB: Npgsql.PostgresException from IActivityLogService.ListAsync(Page = 80_000_000). It surfaces as an unhandled 500, because neither DomainExceptionPageFilter nor ApiExceptionFilter maps PostgresException. Before this phase the paging ran in memory, where a negative Skip was harmless.
confirmed.fix: Compute the offset in long and short-circuit: if (long)(page-1)*pageSize >= total, return an empty page without querying. Or clamp page to ceil(total/pageSize) before calling Skip.

confirmed.title: Offline replay drops the owner's queued work on 401/403 and antiforgery 400 (expired session or another user signed in from another tab)
confirmed.scenario: Case 1: a warehouse phone stays offline longer than the 8 h cookie lifetime. On reconnect, flush() gets 401 from the API, treats it as «سرور تصمیم گرفته» and removes every queued action permanently. Case 2: tab 1 (user A) holds A's queue; in tab 2, A signs out and B signs in. Tab 1's 'online' event replays A's actions with B's cookie and A's stale CSRF token. Antiforgery rejects them with 400 and all of A's items are deleted from A's key, even though A's work never reached the server. Per-user scoping is meant to keep that work for A.
confirmed.fix: In flush(), treat 401, 403 and 400-without-body (antiforgery) as stop-and-keep, like a network error: break, keep the item and surface «دوباره وارد شوید». Optionally confirm that GET /api/me's userId matches the queue scope before replaying.

Confirmed at 2b5870c. In flush(), every response that isn't ok is treated as "the server decided": the item is removed at offlineQueue.ts:200-201 and only a toast is shown. A 401 is not a decision about the action, but it is dropped the same way. Nothing else in the client or on the server stops this.

How Case 1 happens:
- The cookie expires after 8 h (sliding), or SecurityStampValidator rejects it (for example after an admin resets the password or changes the role while the phone is offline).
- The page stays open, and the queued quick-advance POST is replayed by the 'online' event or by the «ارسال حالا» button.
- The POST goes to /api/rugs/{id}/steps/{stepId}/advance, which sits under ApiControllerBase with [Authorize(Policy=Floor)].
- Program.cs:119-129 answers /api paths with 401 and JSON {message: SessionExpiredMessage} instead of a redirect.
- flush() reads that message, pushes it to rejected and calls remove(action.id), which persists the shorter queue to A's scoped key.
- The toast tells the user to refresh and sign in again. After they sign in, the queue is empty, so the step completion is lost.

How Case 2 happens:
- Tab 1 still has A's appContext and A's CSRF meta token.
- After B signs in from another tab, a replay from tab 1 is checked by [AutoValidateAntiforgeryToken] (ApiControllerBase.cs:20). The token was issued for A's claims, so it fails against B's identity and returns 400.
- The item is then removed from A's key.
- One correction to the report: because of [ApiController], the 400 carries a ProblemDetails body, not an empty one. flush() just falls back to its generic message, so the outcome is the same.
- Case 2 needs A's items to still be queued while the network works for B's sign-in. That happens when items were queued on a fetch TypeError with navigator.onLine already true, so no 'online' transition flushed them. The replay then comes from a manual retry or a later 'online' event in tab 1. This is narrow but reachable.

Case 1 is the clear, realistic path. Severity low is fair: the work is a re-doable step completion, and a toast does appear.

confirmed.title: offline.html never gets the self-hosted Vazirmatn font: it asks for an unversioned stylesheet URL that the service worker never caches
confirmed.scenario: The layout, Help/Card and Sales/Print all load `~/fonts/vazirmatn.css` with asp-append-version, so the browser requests `/fonts/vazirmatn.css?v=<hash>` and the service worker's cache-first branch (sw.js:54) stores it under that exact URL. The woff2 file is cached too. The user then goes offline and navigates. sw.js:70 serves the precached /offline.html, which requests `/fonts/vazirmatn.css` with no query string. caches.match(request) treats the query string as part of the key (ignoreSearch defaults to false), so it misses. The fetch fails, `.catch(() => cached)` resolves to undefined, and the stylesheet load fails. The page falls back to Tahoma/sans-serif, which contradicts the P1 brief ('offline.html: use the self-hosted font') and the file's own comment. The stylesheet is not in PRECACHE either (sw.js:16-23). I could not run this in the browser because the pane cannot register service workers. It follows directly from the Cache API key rules and is the only unversioned reference (git grep vazirmatn.css).
confirmed.fix: Add '/fonts/vazirmatn.css' and '/fonts/Vazirmatn-Variable.woff2' to PRECACHE in sw.js and bump CACHE to 'rugs-static-v5'. Alternatively, for /fonts/ requests use caches.match(request, { ignoreSearch: true }).

rejected.title: Nobody can change a Merchant's or Operator's UiMode: PUT /api/me/preferences drops it and returns 204, and there is no admin path either
rejected.why:
The finding describes the code accurately, but the behaviour is a deliberate, documented design that fits the spec and the P1 brief. It is not a defect.

At 2b5870c, UserPreferencesService.cs:74 writes UiMode only for a TenantAdmin. This restriction is stated in several places: the UpdateMyPreferencesRequest doc (UserPreferencesDtos.cs:20,26), IUserPreferencesService.cs:17, MeApiController.cs:35 and lib/types/platform.ts:142. UsersController.cs:19 says the per-role default mode and text size are set by the service at creation and on a role change. So the only writer for Merchants and Operators is User.ApplyRoleDefaultPreferences, by design.

The spec does not require anything more for P1:
- A.1 fixes the personas: Merchant is Simple, Operator is Simple, and TenantAdmin is Full with a «نمای ساده» preview toggle. A.3 gives only the per-role defaults. Neither says a Merchant or Operator can switch to Full.
- I.2 marks uiMode on the Floor endpoint as optional ("uiMode?") and does not say which roles it is accepted from. TenantAdmin also passes the Floor policy, so the shared endpoint does not imply every role may set it.
- The P1 brief scopes the UiMode work in UserManagementService to "UiMode default by role".
- The P1 acceptance list only requires that "The text scale persists". That works: TextScale is accepted from every role.
- The spec walkthrough step 1 ("Create «پدر» as Merchant with «نمای ساده»") is met by the default; the P1 integration report confirms new Merchants get Simple + Large.

No shipped client sends uiMode. ui.ts:439 and site.js:379 send only textScale, and HomeCoach.island.vue:64 sends only dismissCoach. No .vue file or Razor view has a mode control. So the "204 hides the dropped value" case needs a hand-crafted API call, and the result is the documented "ignored" outcome. No UI is misled.

The checklist step that refers to the Merchant's mode (H.9 #5, «merchantUser», linking to /Users) belongs to P7, and the restriction cannot fail it: Merchants are always Simple.

The only real inaccuracy is the stale comment at UserPreferencesService.cs:72-73. It says the TenantAdmin sets these modes from the Users page, and no such control exists. That is a documentation nit, not wrong behaviour. | The mechanics the finding describes are accurate, but they are the intended, documented and tested behaviour, and they do not break anything the spec or the P1 brief requires. So this is not a real defect.

1. Behaviour confirmed by trace. UserPreferencesService.cs:74 writes UiMode only when `user.Role == UserRole.TenantAdmin`. MeApiController.UpdatePreferences always returns 204. UpdateUserRequest(FullName, Role, IsActive, NewPassword) has no UiMode field. The only other place that writes UiMode is User.ApplyRoleDefaultPreferences, which runs on create and on a role change. No build was needed: the unit test PlatformServicesTests.MyPreferences_UiMode_IsHonouredOnlyForTenantAdmin (tests/RugsManagment.Tests/PlatformServicesTests.cs:307-321) asserts exactly this. A Merchant or Operator who sends Full keeps their old mode.

2. The behaviour is deliberate and part of the API contract. The MeApiController doc comment (lines 29-35), the UpdateMyPreferencesRequest doc and the TypeScript type (ClientApp/src/lib/types/platform.ts:141-147) all state that `uiMode` is accepted only from the TenantAdmin and ignored for other roles.

3. The spec does not require the missing capability.
   - A.3 gives only role defaults: Simple for Merchant and Operator, Full for TenantAdmin. The only mode toggle it describes is the TenantAdmin's previewSimple.
   - I.2 writes the body as `{textScale, gridEnter, uiMode?}`. Only uiMode carries the `?`, which fits conditional acceptance. Nothing in it says every Floor role may change its mode.
   - The P1 brief limits UserManagementService to "Merchant role allowed; UiMode default by role".
   - No section of the spec, in any phase, asks for a UiMode control on the Users page.

4. Nothing in the app can produce the "silently dropped" case. No client code at 2b5870c ever sends `uiMode` for any role. TextScaleControl/ui.ts sends only textScale, HomeCoach sends only dismissCoach, and site.js sends textScale and previewSimple. So a Merchant or Operator never sees a mode switch fail; the case is reachable only with a hand-written API call, and the API docs describe that response.

What remains is a feature the spec never asked for: a Merchant or Operator cannot be moved to Full mode. The comment saying the TenantAdmin sets these modes on the Users page is inaccurate, but that is a documentation slip, not a behaviour failure.

rejected.title: Dismissing the Home coach with the keyboard drops focus to <body>
rejected.why: The finding's failure, where the next Tab starts again from the skip link, does not happen in Chromium. Chromium keeps the sequential focus navigation starting point where the removed button was. After «بعداً» or «فهمیدم» removes the coach section, the next Tab goes to the first focusable element after the coach, which is the first home tile. One part of the finding is true: document.activeElement does become BODY. That is ordinary browser behaviour, and it is not the keyboard failure the finding claims. The spec also does not require what the finding says it does. H.7 asks for managed focus only for dialogs and drawers (Esc closes, focus returns to the opener). Its "New controls" list covers radiogroups, the meter, readiness chips and 44 px targets. It says nothing about inline dismissible sections like the Home coach. | The finding is half right, and the half that matters is wrong. When the coach closes, document.activeElement does become BODY. At 2b5870c, later() (line 58) and the finally block of dismiss() (line 69) set visible=false. The v-if at line 76 then removes the section that held the focused button, and nothing else in the codebase moves focus anywhere (I searched for activeElement, focusout and MutationObserver and found nothing that does). What is wrong is the failure the finding reports: that the next Tab starts again at the skip link. Chromium remembers where the removed element was (its "sequential focus navigation starting point"), so the next Tab goes to the first focusable element after the coach, which is the first home tile, exactly where a keyboard user would expect to go. Firefox and Safari behave the same way, from memory; I did not test them. Spec H.7 also never requires managed focus for an inline card like the coach. It asks only that dialogs and drawers reuse UiShell's focus trap and return focus to the opener on Esc. So no stated requirement is broken, and the concrete failure scenario did not happen when tested.
